proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I keep telling myself I'll sort my finances next month?"
pubDate: 2026-07-01
description: "You're not lazy. You're doing exactly what a human brain does when a cost feels abstract and the present feels loud. Here's what's actually happening in that moment."
tags: ["money avoidance", "behavioural economics", "self-awareness"]
---

There is a tab I kept open for eleven months.

It was my tax return. I am a qualified financial planner. I teach people about money for a living. The tab sat there, minimised, behind everything else, and every time I saw the favicon I told myself: next week, when things are quieter.

Things were never quieter. That is not a coincidence.

Behavioural economists call this present bias: the brain assigns disproportionate weight to right now, and discounts future consequences in a way that feels completely rational in the moment. The tax return cost was real but abstract. The discomfort of opening it was real and immediate. So I did not open it.

If you earn reasonably well and still find yourself thinking "I'll set up that ISA in September" or "I'll look at my pension contributions when I'm less busy," you are not disorganised. You are doing exactly what a human brain does under conditions of vague future cost and sharp present discomfort.

The thing worth examining is not whether you are doing this. You are. The question is what the delay is actually protecting you from.

For a lot of people I work with, "next month" is not laziness. It is a quiet agreement not to look too closely, because looking closely might reveal a gap between where they are and where they believed they would be by now. That gap has feelings attached to it. Present bias gives you a socially acceptable reason to keep the tab minimised.

The first step is not a spreadsheet. It is noticing that the delay is doing a job, and asking what job that is.

If you want to understand your own pattern around this, the free quiz at [link] takes four minutes and gives you a specific, grounded starting point.

Joel Humphrey, MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner
